code.title: Check API data at run time

followUps:
You write a check by hand, or use a schema library, that runs in the browser. TypeScript only trusts what you tell it, and JSON.parse or response.json() returns any.

Parse the response as unknown, then run a guard or a schema (Zod, Valibot) that checks each field. If it passes, you get a typed value; if not, you report an error. Cost is O(fields) per response.

It turns on a group of strict checks at once, so the compiler catches far more mistakes. The main ones are strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, strictFunctionTypes, strictPropertyInitialization and useUnknownInCatchVariables.

Example: with strictNullChecks, let s: string = null is an error, and user.name is an error if user may be undefined. Start every new project with "strict": true.

Yes, in recent versions. Node 22.18 and later (and Node 23.6+) can run .ts files by stripping the types, with no flag needed; older versions need a tool such as tsx or ts-node.

Limits: Node only erases types, it does not check them, so you still run tsc --noEmit in CI. Syntax that needs code generation, such as enums and parameter properties, needs a special flag or must be avoided. Use import type for type-only imports.

code.title: unknown, never and void in action

followUps:
object means any non-primitive value (arrays and functions too), {} means any value except null and undefined (so even a number fits), and Record<string, unknown> means a plain dictionary with string keys.

Use Record<string, unknown> when you want to read keys safely. Avoid {} and Object because they accept things like 5 and "hi". For an unknown JSON object, Record<string, unknown> is the usual choice.

A tuple is better when the position carries the meaning, the length is fixed and short, and the caller will destructure it right away. React's useState returns [value, setValue] for this reason.

Example: type Point = [number, number] is fine, but a record with id, name, email should be an object because names are clearer than positions. Rule of thumb: more than two or three items, use an object.

code.title: Interface merging vs type aliases

followUps:
It is useful when you add to a type you do not own. You reopen the same interface name in another file and the members are merged.

Real examples: adding a field to Express's Request (user after authentication), extending Window with a global such as window.appConfig, or adding keys to a library's options interface. In your own code, avoid it; it makes types hard to find.

? marks a property as optional (it may be missing, so its type becomes T | undefined), and readonly means you cannot assign to it after the object is created.

Example: interface User { readonly id: number; nickname?: string }. u.id = 2 is a compile error; u.nickname may be undefined. Both exist only at compile time; at run time the object can still be changed unless you use Object.freeze.

A common bug is passing a method as a callback: setTimeout(user.greet, 0). When the timer calls it, this is no longer user, so this.name is undefined (or it throws in strict mode).

Fixes: an arrow function () => user.greet(), user.greet.bind(user), or define the method as an arrow-function property. Arrow functions keep the this of where they were written.

Hoisting means declarations are moved to the top of their scope before the code runs. function declarations are fully usable before their line; var is hoisted as undefined; let and const are hoisted but sit in a "temporal dead zone", so using them early throws a ReferenceError.

Example: console.log(a); var a = 1; prints undefined, while the same with let throws. Prefer const and let.

Compare field by field, because === on objects compares references, not contents. For small flat objects, check the keys and values in a loop; for nested data, write a recursive function or use a library such as lodash isEqual.

Quick but fragile trick: JSON.stringify(a) === JSON.stringify(b); it depends on key order and drops undefined, functions and dates. Newer runtimes also have structuredClone, but that copies, it does not compare.

code.title: Generics with constraints and keyof

followUps:
keyof T gives a union of the property names of T as string literals. For { id: number; name: string } it is "id" | "name".

It lets a function accept only valid keys: function get<T, K extends keyof T>(o: T, k: K): T[K]. Calling get(user, "emial") is a compile error, and the return type follows the key you pass. The check is compile-time only.

A generic adds no value when the type parameter appears only once, so it does not connect two things. function log<T>(x: T): void is the same as function log(x: unknown): void.

A generic earns its place when it links input to output or two arguments together, such as function first<T>(a: T[]): T | undefined. If you cannot say what the parameter ties together, remove it. Extra generics make signatures harder to read.

TypeScript generics are erased, so at run time there is only one version of the code and nothing knows what T was. C# generics are kept by the .NET runtime, so List<int> and List<string> are real different types.

Result: in TypeScript you cannot write new T(), typeof T or x instanceof T. You must pass a value (such as a class constructor) if you need it at run time.

code.title: Discriminated union with exhaustive check

followUps:
The compiler would trust the lie, so a wrong guard creates bugs that the types cannot see. A guard x is User only returns a boolean; TypeScript does not check that your test matches the type.

Example: isUser = (x): x is User => typeof x === "object" passes for {}, and later user.name.length crashes. Keep guards complete (check every field), and test them, or use a schema library which does this for you.

TypeScript cannot be sure a variable stays the same when a callback runs later, so it forgets the narrowing for let variables and mutable properties.

Example: after if (user.name) { a callback passed to setTimeout may see user.name as string | undefined again. Fix by copying into a const first: const name = user.name;. Narrowing of const values is kept.

code.title: Utility types as object helpers

followUps:
Partial<T> is a mapped type that adds ? to every property:

type Partial<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] };

It loops over every key of T and makes it optional. Required<T> is the same with -?, and Readonly<T> adds readonly. It is shallow: nested objects are not changed.

Omit works on object types and removes properties by key. Exclude works on unions and removes members of the union.

Example: Omit<User, "password"> gives the user without that field. Exclude<"a" | "b" | "c", "a"> gives "b" | "c". Mixing them up is a common mistake; the partner of Pick is Omit, the partner of Extract is Exclude.

Shallow. Readonly<T> only marks the top-level properties as read-only; objects and arrays inside can still be changed.

Example: with Readonly<{ tags: string[] }>, o.tags = [] is an error but o.tags.push("x") is allowed. For deep protection, write a recursive DeepReadonly or use readonly string[] on the inner types. It is also compile-time only; use Object.freeze for run time.

code.title: as const, satisfies and erased casts

followUps:
as is acceptable when you know more than the compiler and cannot express it in types: for example, document.getElementById("app") as HTMLCanvasElement, or after a check that TypeScript cannot follow.

It is not acceptable to silence an error you do not understand, or to cast API data to a type without checking. as does no run-time work. Prefer a type guard or a schema; keep a comment when you must use it.

Declare the array with as const and take the element type with typeof arr[number].

const ROLES = ["admin", "user"] as const;
type Role = typeof ROLES[number]; // "admin" | "user"

The array also exists at run time, so you can loop over it or check ROLES.includes(x), and the union stays in sync automatically.

code.title: Strict null checks and unknown in catch

followUps:
Turn on one flag at a time, and let the build keep passing while you fix each one. Start with noImplicitAny, then strictNullChecks, which usually finds the most errors.

Options: enable flags per step in separate pull requests; use a second tsconfig.strict.json that lists already-clean folders; or use // @ts-expect-error on known failures with a tracked ticket. Add a CI check so the error count only goes down.

Because anything can be thrown in JavaScript, not only Error objects: throw "oops" and throw 42 are legal. Typing it as any would hide that.

With unknown you must check first: if (e instanceof Error) console.log(e.message). It is on by default with strict (useUnknownInCatchVariables). A small helper such as getMessage(e: unknown): string keeps catch blocks short.

code.title: Abstract class and private fields

followUps:
Use an interface when you only need a contract, with no shared code. Use an abstract class when subclasses should share real code or state and you want to force them to implement a few methods.

An interface costs nothing at run time and a class can implement many interfaces, but it can extend only one class. In front-end code, interfaces and plain functions are the common choice; abstract classes are rare.

A parameter property is a shortcut: constructor(private http: HttpClient) {} declares the field and assigns it in one line.

Some teams ban it because it needs real code to be generated (so it fails with Node's type-stripping and the erasableSyntaxOnly option) and it hides the field list. With Angular, the inject() function in a field initializer is the modern replacement, and it avoids this syntax.

Angular's decorators like @Injectable() and @Component() attach metadata to the class. The compiler uses it, together with the constructor parameter types (or inject()), to know which service to build and pass in.

Example: @Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' }) tells Angular to create one shared instance. Without the decorator, Angular would not know how to build the class. Note that Angular's decorators are separate from the newer standard JavaScript decorators.

Because the dev server (Vite, esbuild) only strips the types and does not check them. It is fast because it never type-checks.

So type errors appear in the editor and in the terminal or CI only if you run tsc --noEmit. Always add that command to the pipeline and to a pre-push check, or errors will slip into main. Angular's own build does check types.

Path aliases let you write import { Button } from "@ui/button" instead of "../../../ui/button". You set them in tsconfig.json under compilerOptions.paths (with baseUrl or relative targets).

TypeScript only uses them for type checking; the bundler must know them too, for example Vite's resolve.alias, a plugin, or Jest's moduleNameMapper. If one is missing the build or the tests fail.

After the current synchronous code finishes, as a microtask. await x pauses the function; the rest runs when x settles, but still before any timer.

console.log(1);
setTimeout(() => console.log(4));
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(3));
console.log(2); // prints 1 2 3 4

Debounce waits until the events stop, then runs once (search box: run after the user stops typing for 300 ms). Throttle runs at most once per time window, however many events come (scroll handler: at most once every 100 ms).

Use debounce when only the last value matters; use throttle when you want regular updates during a continuous action.

|| returns the right side for any falsy value, and 0 is falsy. So count || 10 gives 10 when count is 0, which is probably wrong.

Use the nullish operator ??, which only replaces null and undefined: count ?? 10 gives 0. The same trap applies to "" and false.

code.title: Enum vs as const object

followUps:
A numeric enum compiles to an object that maps both ways: name to number and number to name. For enum Level { Low, High } you get Level.Low === 0 and Level[0] === "Low".

That lets you print a readable name from a stored number. String enums do not get a reverse mapping. A downside: any number is assignable to a numeric enum in older versions, so prefer string literal unions.

Keep the values in an array with as const and derive the type from it, then loop over the array.

const SIZES = ["s", "m", "l"] as const;
type Size = typeof SIZES[number];
for (const s of SIZES) console.log(s);

A pure union type such as "s" | "m" | "l" cannot be looped over because types are erased.

code.title: Validate an API response

followUps:
Yes. Front-end validation is for the user's comfort; it can be skipped by anyone using the browser tools, curl or a script. The API must never trust the client.

The server checks length, format, ranges, permissions and business rules (for example "email is unique") and returns clear errors (400 or 422 with a field list). Ideally share the rules or generate them from the same contract, so the two sides do not drift apart.

Do not crash: decide what an unknown value means. Either reject it with a clear message, or map it to a safe "unknown" case and show a neutral label.

Example: the server adds status "refunded". The old client has switch with a default branch that shows "Other" and logs a warning. Agree with the API team to add values compatibly (additive change, new version header, or release the client first).

Trust the contract, but verify at run time. Generated types (from OpenAPI) stay in sync with the server, which is their big advantage, yet they are still erased and do not check live data.

Best mix: generate the types and schemas from the OpenAPI document, then run the schema at the boundary. Hand-written schemas drift. For trusted internal services you may skip run-time checks, but keep them for public or third-party data.

code.title: Typed client with one shared token refresh

followUps:
Retry only calls that are safe to repeat, and only for temporary failures: network errors, 502, 503, 504, and 429 (respecting Retry-After). Use exponential backoff with jitter and a small limit, for example 3 tries.

GET, PUT and DELETE are meant to be idempotent. A POST such as "create order" is not, unless it carries an idempotency key that the server checks. Never retry 400 or 401/403 blindly.

Keep one shared "refresh in progress" promise. The first 401 starts the refresh and stores the promise; every other request that gets a 401 awaits the same promise, then retries once with the new token.

refreshing ??= doRefresh().finally(() => refreshing = null);
await refreshing; // everyone waits for one call

This prevents ten refresh calls and the race where the refresh token is used twice.

Usually yes. If the API has an OpenAPI (Swagger) document, which .NET 9 and 10 can produce, generate the types and client with a tool such as openapi-typescript, NSwag or Orval.

You get less hand-written code and the compiler flags changes when the API changes. Wrap the generated client in a thin layer for auth, retry and error mapping. Hand-write only for small APIs or when generated code is too noisy.

code.title: DeepPartial applied at run time

followUps:
infer declares a type variable inside a conditional type and lets TypeScript fill it in by pattern matching.

type ElementOf<T> = T extends (infer U)[] ? U : never;
type A = ElementOf<string[]>; // string

The built-in ReturnType<F> and Awaited<T> use it. It only works inside the extends part of a conditional type.

When a conditional type is applied to a naked type parameter that is a union, it is applied to each member separately and the results are joined.

type ToArray<T> = T extends any ? T[] : never;
type R = ToArray<string | number>; // string[] | number[]

To stop this, wrap both sides in a tuple: [T] extends [any]. This is also how Exclude works.

Make a mapped type that calls itself for object properties.

type DeepPartial<T> = {
  [K in keyof T]?: T[K] extends object ? DeepPartial<T[K]> : T[K];
};

Caution: arrays and functions are also objects, so you may need extra cases for them. It is useful for patch or config objects where nested fields can be left out.

code.title: Structural typing and branded ids

followUps:
Without the check, a typo in an object literal would silently be accepted, because extra properties are normally allowed in structural typing. The check catches typos where you clearly meant to fill exactly this type.

Example: const o: { color?: string } = { colour: "red" } is an error. It applies only to fresh object literals, not to variables, which is why the same object passed through a variable compiles.

Do the check in one place, a small function that validates the plain value and then casts it, and make the brand type impossible to create in any other way.

type UserId = number & { readonly __brand: "UserId" };
function toUserId(n: number): UserId {
  if (!Number.isInteger(n) || n <= 0) throw new Error("bad id");
  return n as UserId;
}

The brand exists only in the type system; at run time it is just a number.

Make it visible and tie it to normal work. Keep a dashboard of the number of files still in JavaScript or with errors, review it every sprint, and set a rule: every pull request that touches a file converts it (the "boy scout" rule).

Also assign a named owner, set a target date, and protect finished folders with a stricter tsconfig in CI so they cannot go backwards. Celebrate milestones; the last 20 percent is often the hardest code, so schedule it explicitly.

First look for the types package @types/name. If none exists, write a small declare module "name" file with only the parts you use, and contribute it upstream if useful.

The quick fallback is declare module "name";, which makes everything any; use it only as a temporary step with a ticket. Wrap the library in your own typed module so the untyped area stays small and in one place.

Choose measures before you start. Good ones: production errors of type "undefined is not a function" per month, time to fix bugs, how often changes break the build later, and developer survey scores on confidence when refactoring.

Also count the migration's cost, such as hours spent. Compare a few months before and after. Do not rely only on the number of converted files, since that measures activity, not benefit.

code.title: Virtual DOM diff: re-render without DOM change

followUps:
No. A re-render only runs your component function again to produce a new description of the screen. React then compares it with the previous one and changes the real DOM only where something differs.

Example: a parent re-renders with the same text in a <p>; the function runs, but the DOM node is untouched. This is why re-renders are usually cheap, and why fixing them is only needed when the render work itself is slow.

Because React may call your component more than once, pause it, or throw the result away (Strict Mode even calls it twice on purpose in development). If rendering has side effects, such as changing a global or sending a request, the result becomes unpredictable.

Rule: same props, state and context give the same output, and nothing outside is changed. Put side effects in event handlers or useEffect.

A key tells React which item in a list is which across renders, so it can keep the right state and DOM node when items move, are added or removed.

Use a stable unique id (such as the database id). With index keys, deleting the first row makes React reuse row 0's state for the old row 1, and typed text jumps to the wrong row. Changing a component's key also resets it completely.

code.title: State snapshots and functional updates

followUps:
children is the content placed between a component's opening and closing tags, passed in as a normal prop.

function Card({ children }) { return <div className="card">{children}</div>; }
// <Card><p>Hello</p></Card>

It lets a component wrap anything without knowing what it is, and is the basis for layouts, modals and context providers. In TypeScript the type is ReactNode.

Use it when the new value depends on the old one. setCount(c => c + 1) always receives the latest value, while setCount(count + 1) uses the value from the current render.

Example: calling setCount(count + 1) twice in one handler with count 0 gives 1; calling setCount(c => c + 1) twice gives 2. It is also needed inside timers and async callbacks, where the captured value is old.

You should not. Props are read-only, and React expects a child to treat them as input only. Assigning to a prop is a bug; in dev it may even throw because props are frozen.

If the child needs to cause a change, the parent passes a callback prop (onChange) and the child calls it. If the child needs its own editable copy, it keeps that copy in its own state, initialized from the prop.

With index keys, React matches items by position. When you delete or reorder rows, state and DOM of one row can end up attached to a different item. Typical symptom: after deleting row 1, an input still shows row 1's typed text on the next row.

Use a stable id from the data. Index keys are fine only for a static list that never reorders or changes.

When you only need the value at submit time and do not react to every keystroke: a simple search form, a file input (which is always uncontrolled), or integrating with a non-React library. Read it with a ref or from FormData.

It means fewer re-renders and less code. Choose controlled inputs when you need live validation, formatting, or a value that other parts of the screen depend on.

Prop drilling is passing props through many levels of components that do not use them, just to reach a deep child. It makes code noisy and hard to change.

Options: composition (pass the finished element as children), context for values like theme or current user, or a state library. Do not reach for context for everything, as one or two levels of passing is perfectly fine.

code.title: JSX becomes function calls

followUps:
class is a reserved word in JavaScript, and JSX is JavaScript. React uses the DOM property name, which is className, the same name as in element.className.

Similar renames: htmlFor instead of for, and camelCase for attributes like onClick and tabIndex. Attributes such as aria-label and data-id keep their dashes.

No. A browser understands only JavaScript, so JSX must be turned into function calls first by a compiler such as Babel, SWC, esbuild or the TypeScript compiler.

Example: <h1 id="t">Hi</h1> becomes jsx("h1", { id: "t", children: "Hi" }). Your build tool does this automatically, so you rarely see the output.

With a .tsx file, the compiler reads the props type of the component function and checks every attribute in the tag against it. A missing required prop, a wrong type or an unknown attribute is a compile error.

type Props = { label: string; onClick: () => void };
const Button = ({ label, onClick }: Props) => ...
// <Button label={5} />  error: number is not string

code.title: Why hooks cannot be conditional

followUps:
React remembers hook values by the order of the calls, in a list. If a hook runs only sometimes, the order shifts and each later hook reads another hook's value.

Example: render 1 calls useState three times; render 2 skips the middle one, so the third call gets the second slot's value. So hooks must run in the same order on every render: only at the top level, never in if, loops, or after an early return.

Choose useReducer when the next state depends on several fields, when many different actions change the same state, or when you want the update logic in one testable function.

Example: a form with loading, error and data fields, or a cart with add, remove and clear actions. A reducer (state, action) => newState is a pure function, easy to unit test. For one independent value, useState is simpler.

It should stop the old request from changing state after the component has gone or the input has changed. Use an AbortController and abort it in the cleanup, or set an ignore flag.

useEffect(() => {
  const ctrl = new AbortController();
  fetch(url, { signal: ctrl.signal }).then(r => r.json()).then(setData);
  return () => ctrl.abort();
}, [url]);

Without it, a slow old response can overwrite a newer one (a race).

code.title: Custom hook with its own state

followUps:
Test it through a component that uses it, or with renderHook from React Testing Library. You call actions inside act() and check the returned value.

const { result } = renderHook(() => useToggle());
act(() => result.current[1]());
expect(result.current[0]).toBe(true);

For hooks that call APIs, mock the network (for example with MSW) instead of mocking the hook's internals.

Lift the state up to a common parent and pass it down, or put it in context or a store. A custom hook shares logic, not state: each component that calls it gets its own separate copy of the state.

Example: two components calling useToggle() have two independent switches. If both must show the same value, the hook should read from a shared source such as a context.

Prefer custom hooks. They are plain functions, they compose easily, and they avoid the "wrapper hell" and prop-name clashes of higher-order components (HOCs).

HOCs still make sense for wrapping a component with something that must be applied from outside, such as an error boundary or legacy class components that cannot use hooks. In new code, a hook is the default way to reuse logic.

code.title: Store with selectors

followUps:
Split the context into small pieces, or keep fast-changing and slow-changing values in different contexts. Every consumer re-renders when the value of its context changes.

Other fixes: memoize the context value (useMemo), put the provider as low as possible, pass elements as children so they are not re-created, or use a store with selectors (Zustand, Redux) so each component listens only to its slice.

Redux Toolkit removes the boilerplate: createSlice writes actions and reducers together, Immer lets you write "mutating" code that is safely turned into immutable updates, and configureStore sets up dev tools and sensible middleware.

RTK Query adds data fetching and caching. Today plain Redux is not recommended; Toolkit is the official way.

Server state is a copy of data that lives on the server: it can become stale, other users can change it, and it needs loading, error and refresh handling. Client state, such as an open dropdown or a draft, belongs only to the browser.

Treat them differently: use a cache library (TanStack Query, RTK Query) for server state, with refetching and invalidation, and local state or a small store for client state.

code.title: Controlled form with double-submit guard

followUps:
Return field errors from the API in a standard shape, for example a 400 or 422 response with a problem+json body that has an errors map: { "email": ["already used"] }. In the form, map each key to the matching field and show the message beside it.

With React Hook Form that is setError("email", { message }). Keep the field names identical on both sides, and also show a general error at the top for messages without a field.

Disable the submit button while the request runs and ignore a second call in the handler. Use a flag from state (isSubmitting) or, better, the pending state of a mutation or action.

A button can still be clicked twice quickly before the state updates, so also guard with a ref. For payments or orders, send an idempotency key so the server ignores a repeated request.

In React 19, useActionState(action, initialState) returns three things: the current state, a wrapped action to pass to <form action={...}>, and an isPending flag.

const [state, formAction, isPending] = useActionState(save, { error: null });

The action receives the previous state and the FormData, and whatever it returns becomes the new state, so server errors can be shown without extra code.

code.title: Error boundary around a failing widget

followUps:
Log it to your monitoring service from the boundary's componentDidCatch(error, info) method, or from the onError callbacks in React 19's root options (onCaughtError, onUncaughtError).

Send the message, stack, the component stack from info, the app version and the user or session id (without private data). Tools like Sentry or Application Insights have ready-made integrations.

Put them around parts that load data or code on their own, so one slow part does not block the page: one around each route, and one around heavy independent widgets like a chart or table. Each needs a good fallback (a skeleton).

Avoid one huge boundary at the root, because the whole page then shows a spinner. Put an error boundary next to each Suspense boundary to catch failures.

Because the code runs in the user's browser, and the user can change it, skip it or call your API directly. A route guard only hides screens; it does not protect data.

The real check must happen on the server for every request: validate the token, then check the role and ownership. Use guards for good user experience (redirect to login), never as the only barrier.

If you test internal state, a harmless refactor (renaming a variable or switching to a reducer) breaks the test even though the screen behaves the same. The test is tied to how it works, not what it does.

Test what the user sees and does: render, click, type, and check text on the screen with Testing Library queries like getByRole. Then tests survive refactoring and also prove accessibility to some extent.

Do not use fixed sleeps. Wait for the actual result with await screen.findByText(...) or waitFor, mock the network with MSW so timing is controlled, and use fake timers for debounce and timeouts.

Other causes: tests sharing state (reset between tests), real dates and random values (fix them), and animations. A flaky test should be fixed or removed quickly, since it teaches people to ignore red builds.

Only in a limited way. They catch accidental changes in small, stable output such as an icon or a formatted string, but large snapshots are accepted without reading, so they protect little.

Better: explicit assertions on what matters. If you keep snapshots, keep them small and review the diff in every pull request. For visual checks, a screenshot tool such as Playwright's comparison or Chromatic is more useful.

Use a linter (eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y) in the editor and CI, run jest-axe or axe in component tests, and run Playwright tests with @axe-core/playwright on key pages. Lighthouse in CI is a useful extra check.

Automation finds roughly a third to half of issues (missing labels, low contrast). You still need keyboard-only testing and a screen reader check (NVDA or VoiceOver) on main flows.

CSP is a response header that tells the browser which sources of scripts, styles and connections are allowed. It limits the damage of cross-site scripting (XSS): if an attacker injects a script tag, the browser refuses to run it when it is not from an allowed source.

Example: script-src 'self' 'nonce-...'. It does not replace escaping and input handling; it is a second layer. React already escapes text by default.

Avoid it if you can. Two libraries mean larger bundles, two looks, two accessibility behaviours and two upgrade paths.

If you must (for example a data grid from one and forms from another), choose one as the base, wrap each component in your own thin design-system layer, share theme tokens (colors, spacing, fonts), and set a rule on where the second is allowed. Document it so teams do not keep adding libraries.

When the calculation is cheap, or the result is used by components that re-render anyway. useMemo itself costs memory and a comparison of dependencies, so for a simple sum or a small filter it can be slower than recomputing.

Use it for genuinely expensive work (sorting 10,000 rows), or to keep a stable reference passed to a memoized child. Measure with the Profiler first.

No. A Server Component runs only on the server and sends no JavaScript to the browser, so it cannot handle events or hold state. An onClick needs a Client Component, marked with "use client".

The usual pattern: a Server Component fetches data and renders a small Client Component for the interactive part, passing data as props.

The React Compiler (stable since React 19.x) adds memoization automatically at build time, so you rarely need to write useMemo, useCallback and React.memo by hand.

It requires code to follow the rules of React: pure rendering and no mutation of props or state. Existing manual memoization still works. Turn it on gradually and test.

code.title: Derived state and key reset

followUps:
Because a fetch inside an effect starts only after the first render and paint, can create waterfalls (one request after another), and needs manual handling for races, cleanup, caching, retry and loading states.

A second problem: effects run twice in development Strict Mode, so you see duplicate calls. Use a data library (TanStack Query), a router loader, or a Server Component instead. If you do fetch in an effect, abort the request in the cleanup.

When the key of a component changes, React throws away the old instance and creates a new one, with fresh state.

Example: <ProfileForm key={userId} user={user} /> resets every field when userId changes, without an effect that copies props into state. It is the recommended way to reset state on a change of identity.

Derived state is a value you can calculate from existing state or props, such as a filtered list or a total. Do not store it in its own state; compute it while rendering.

Example: keep items and filter in state, and compute visible = items.filter(...) during render. Storing visible too creates two sources of truth that can disagree.

code.title: Server-state cache with staleTime

followUps:
staleTime is how long fetched data counts as fresh: while fresh, no refetch happens (default 0, so data is stale at once). gcTime (formerly cacheTime) is how long unused data stays in memory after the last component stops using it (default 5 minutes).

Example: staleTime: 60_000 means opening the screen again within a minute shows cached data with no request.

Use the query key. Give each item a key like ["user", id] and, after the edit succeeds, call queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ["user", id] }).

Lists with the key ["users"] can be invalidated separately. You can also update the cache directly with setQueryData for an instant change (optimistic update), and roll back if the request fails.

When the data is tiny and loaded once, such as static config, or when the app has only one or two requests. Also when a framework already provides data loading (route loaders, Server Components).

A library adds a dependency and concepts to learn. For a simple case, a custom hook with fetch and an abort controller may be enough. Choose it once you need caching, refetching, pagination or retries.

code.title: Memo defeated by new object props

followUps:
Check whether its props really stay the same. Usually one prop is a new object, array or function created each time the parent renders, such as style={{...}} or onClick={() => ...}, so the shallow comparison fails.

Also check for children passed as JSX (a new element each time) and a context value that changes. Fix with stable references (useMemo, useCallback, constants outside the component), or use the React Compiler. The Profiler shows "why did this render".

It shows each component as a bar: the width is the time spent rendering it, and a grey bar means it did not render in that commit. Hover to see the render time and the reason it rendered (props, state, hooks changed, or parent rendered).

Look for wide bars and for many components rendering for a small change. Fix the widest ones first, and always measure again after a change.

No. A re-render means React called your component function again. The DOM is updated only when the new output differs from the old one.

Example: a parent state change re-renders 50 children, but if their output is identical, zero DOM nodes change. So a re-render has only the cost of running the function, which matters only when the function is heavy.

code.title: Search and paging with debounce

followUps:
Keep the values in the URL query string (?q=ann&page=2), and read them from there, so they are the single source of truth. Then the page survives a refresh, can be bookmarked or shared, and works with the back button.

In React Router use useSearchParams; in Angular use queryParams. Reset page to 1 when the search changes, and debounce the search input before updating the URL.

Do not load all 50,000 at once. Use server-side paging and filtering so the browser gets 20 to 50 rows per request, and show total count from the API.

If the user needs to scroll through a lot, add virtualization (TanStack Virtual, react-window), which renders only the visible rows. Add database indexes for the search column, and prefer cursor (keyset) paging over big offsets for speed.

Use a cursor or "next page" token instead of page numbers. The list keeps what was loaded and appends the next batch when the user nears the bottom (an IntersectionObserver triggers it). TanStack Query has useInfiniteQuery for this.

Watch out: keep scroll position when going back, avoid duplicates when data changes, give keyboard users a "Load more" button, and consider virtualization if the list gets huge.

Probably not at first. Server Components are most helpful with a framework that supports them (Next.js, React Router framework mode), for public pages needing speed, SEO and less JavaScript.

For an internal app behind login with a separate .NET API, a client-side app (Vite) is simpler: one deployment, no Node server to run, and your API remains the one place for logic. Adopt Server Components only if you see a clear need, such as slow first load.

Usually small. Check these: ref is now a normal prop for function components (no forwardRef needed), and removed APIs like propTypes checks, defaultProps on functions, string refs, legacy context and ReactDOM.render.

Also check that libraries support 19, and that TypeScript types are updated. Upgrade to the latest 18.3 first, fix the deprecation warnings, then move to 19.

The compiler needs components and hooks to be pure and to follow the Rules of React: no mutation of props, state or values read during render, and no side effects while rendering.

If code breaks the rules, the compiler skips that component, so it stays correct but not optimized. Install the ESLint plugin from the React team to find violations before you turn it on, and roll it out per folder.

code.title: Stale closure and its fixes

followUps:
Because the lint rule is right: the effect really uses a value that can change, and ignoring the warning leaves a stale-value bug. It will pass tests and then fail in real use.

Better fixes: add the dependency, use a functional update (setX(x => ...)), store the latest value in a ref, or use useEffectEvent for logic that should read the latest values without re-running. If you must disable it, write a comment that explains why.

Anywhere a callback lives longer than one render: setInterval and setTimeout, event listeners added in an effect, WebSocket handlers, promise .then callbacks, and debounced or memoized functions with missing dependencies.

Example: a click listener registered once with [] dependencies keeps seeing the first count forever. Re-register when the value changes, or read it from a ref.

Not completely. The compiler memoizes values correctly based on what you read in render, but a stale closure caused by a wrong dependency array in an effect or by a long-lived listener can still exist.

The compiler also does not rewrite your effects. So keep following the rule of hooks lint, and use functional updates or refs where the callback must outlive a render.

Each call to context.sync() is a round trip between your add-in and the Office host, which is slow. In a loop it multiplies that delay.

Instead queue many operations on the proxy objects, then call sync() once. Example: set the text of 100 paragraphs, then do one await context.sync(). Use load() to request needed properties together, and avoid calling sync inside the loop.

Use single sign-on: the add-in calls Office.auth.getAccessToken() to get a token for the signed-in user, then sends it to your back end. The back end validates it and uses the on-behalf-of flow (OBO) to get a token for Microsoft Graph or your own API.

If SSO is not available, fall back to a dialog with MSAL. Register the add-in in Microsoft Entra ID and never put secrets in the front end.

For testing, sideload the add-in during development (via the manifest, with a local HTTPS dev server), write unit tests for logic separated from the Office calls, and mock the Office object. Test on each target host (Word desktop, web, Mac).

Deploy the front end like any web app to static hosting over HTTPS, then publish the manifest through the Microsoft 365 admin center (centralized deployment) for the company, or through AppSource.

Hydration is when React attaches event handlers and state to HTML that the server already sent, so the static page becomes interactive. React reuses the existing DOM instead of building it again.

A hydration mismatch happens when the HTML from the server differs from what the client renders first, for example with Date.now(), Math.random() or window checks during render. React warns or re-renders. Fix by making first render the same and moving such values into an effect.

Keep the token handling on the server: store the session in a secure, HttpOnly, SameSite cookie, and check it in middleware or in the server code on each request. Server Components can read the user and decide what to render.

Still check authorization at the data layer, not only in the page. A common pattern for .NET back ends is the BFF (backend for frontend), where the server holds the tokens and the browser never sees them.

Go step by step and keep the app working. First move to a framework with routing (such as Next.js or React Router framework mode) with the existing app as a client-only route. Then convert routes one by one, starting with public pages that need SEO or speed.

Move data fetching to the server where it helps, and keep interactive parts as Client Components. Measure results (load time, Core Web Vitals) after each step and stop when the benefit is gone.

A component has a template and is a visible part of the screen. A directive adds behaviour to an existing element or component and has no template of its own.

Example: @Component for a UserCard that shows data; an attribute directive such as appHighlight that changes the background of any element. Structural directives (the older *ngIf) change the DOM layout; today the built-in @if control flow is used instead.

imports lists the other standalone components, directives, pipes or NgModules whose selectors and names the template of this component uses.

If you use <app-user-card> or the date pipe in a template and do not list it, the compiler reports an error (unknown element). It makes each component say exactly what it depends on, which helps tree shaking and reading.

Not gone, but no longer needed. Since Angular 17+ standalone components are the default, and new projects have no NgModules. Old modules still work, and the two styles can be mixed during migration.

Bootstrapping uses bootstrapApplication with provideRouter, provideHttpClient and similar functions. Use the schematic ng generate @angular/core:standalone to migrate.

Because Angular uses the key to know which DOM element matches which item when the list changes, so it can move elements instead of destroying and recreating all of them. The old *ngFor had an optional trackBy, and people often forgot it.

Example: @for (u of users; track u.id) { ... }. Use a stable unique id; track $index is allowed but has the same drawbacks as index keys.

Two-way binding is a property binding plus an event binding. [(ngModel)]="name" is short for [ngModel]="name" (ngModelChange)="name = $event", and it is called "banana in a box".

With signals, Angular has a model() input that works the same way: the parent writes [(value)]="x", and the child can update it. Underneath, the child just emits a change event named valueChange.

The on condition. With @defer (on viewport) it loads when the block scrolls into view; other triggers are on idle (default), on interaction, on hover, on timer(2s), on immediate, or when someCondition.

You can also add @placeholder, @loading and @error blocks. It splits the heavy component into a separate JavaScript chunk, so the first load is smaller.

ngOnChanges. It receives a SimpleChanges object with the previous and current value of each changed input, and runs before ngOnInit and on every later change of an input.

With signal inputs you can replace it with computed or effect, which react automatically when the input changes.

In ngAfterViewInit (or after render with afterNextRender/afterRenderEffect), because only then are the view and its elements created. Use ElementRef or viewChild() to reach them.

Do not touch the DOM in the constructor or ngOnInit, since the elements may not exist, and server-side rendering has no real DOM. Prefer Angular bindings over manual DOM changes.

Content projection lets a parent put its own content inside a child component's template, with <ng-content> as the slot. It is Angular's version of React's children.

<!-- card.html -->  <div class="card"><ng-content /></div>
<!-- use -->  <app-card><p>Hello</p></app-card>

Use select="[header]" for named slots.

Neither is simply faster; the difference is usually small and depends on how the app is written. React re-renders and compares, Angular with signals and OnPush updates only the parts that changed. Bad code is slower in both.

Performance in real apps comes from things like lazy loading, small bundles, virtualized lists, avoiding needless work and good API design. Measure your own screens rather than trust benchmarks.

Choose Angular when you have a large team that needs one clear structure, strict TypeScript, built-in routing, forms, HTTP and DI, and long-term support with regular upgrades. It suits big enterprise apps and teams coming from C# and .NET.

It reduces choice debates because the framework decides most things. Angular's current versions also have signals, standalone components and zoneless mode, so it is modern and fast.

Do not mix them inside one page unless you have to. Keep the front ends separate by area (for example micro-frontends or separate apps behind the same domain), and share a design system built from web components or CSS tokens, plus shared API clients generated from OpenAPI.

Agree on guidelines for auth, logging and testing across both. Allow a second framework only with a good reason, because it doubles training and upgrade work.

code.title: Dependency injection with test override

followUps:
Override the provider in the test setup. In TestBed.configureTestingModule use providers: [{ provide: UserService, useClass: FakeUserService }] or useValue: fake.

For HTTP, use provideHttpClientTesting() and HttpTestingController to answer requests. Because components get dependencies through DI instead of creating them, no code changes are needed.

providers makes a service available to the component, its template and its content children (projected content). viewProviders makes it available only to the component's own view, not to projected content.

It is rarely needed. Use viewProviders when a component must hide an implementation detail from content that the parent projects into it. In everyday work use providers or providedIn: 'root'.

inject() throws an error when it is called outside an injection context, which means outside a constructor or field initializer of a class created by Angular, a factory function, or runInInjectionContext.

Typical mistake: calling inject(Router) inside a click handler or a setTimeout. Fix by calling inject() in a field (private router = inject(Router);) and using the field later.

code.title: Cross-field form validator

followUps:
Add a validator to the FormGroup instead of one control. It gets the whole group, so it can compare fields and return an error object.

const match: ValidatorFn = g =>
  g.get('pw')?.value === g.get('confirm')?.value ? null : { mismatch: true };
this.fb.group({ pw: [''], confirm: [''] }, { validators: match });

Show the message when form.hasError('mismatch'). The error is on the group, not on a field.

Use a FormArray. It holds a list of controls or groups; push() adds a row, removeAt(i) removes one.

get rows() { return this.form.controls.rows; } // FormArray
add() { this.rows.push(this.fb.group({ name: [''] })); }
remove(i: number) { this.rows.removeAt(i); }

In the template loop with @for (row of rows.controls; track row).

value leaves out disabled controls, while getRawValue() includes all controls, enabled or disabled.

Example: a read-only field id is disabled. form.value has no id, but form.getRawValue() does. When you submit the whole object to the API and need that field, use getRawValue().

code.title: Route guards in order

followUps:
canActivate runs after the route is matched and decides whether the user can enter it. canMatch runs earlier, while the router is choosing which route definition matches; if it returns false, the router tries the next route with the same path.

Use canMatch to prevent lazy code from even being downloaded and to give different components to different roles for the same URL. Use canActivate for a simple allow or redirect.

The navigation waits until the resolver finishes, so the user sees the old page or nothing for the whole loading time, and a slow or failed request blocks the navigation.

Often it is better to navigate at once and show a skeleton while data loads in the component (or use withComponentInputBinding and signals). Use a resolver when the page makes no sense without the data, and handle errors.

Inject ActivatedRoute and read paramMap as an observable, or with the router option withComponentInputBinding() declare an @Input() or input() with the same name as the parameter.

id = input.required<string>(); // route /users/:id

Use the observable (not snapshot) when the same component can be reused for different ids.

code.title: Signals, computed and effect

followUps:
A computed is declarative: it recalculates by itself when its inputs change, is cached, and cannot get out of sync. An effect that sets another signal runs later, can cause extra updates and makes the data flow hard to follow.

Example: total = computed(() => price() * qty()) is better than an effect that writes total.set(price() * qty()). Use effects only for side effects such as logging or saving to storage.

A signal always holds a current value you can read synchronously with count(), and the template updates only what depends on it. A BehaviorSubject is an RxJS stream: you subscribe and unsubscribe, and the async pipe or manual handling is needed.

Signals are simpler for local and derived state; RxJS is better for events over time (debounce, retry, cancel). Convert with toSignal and toObservable.

linkedSignal is a writable signal whose value resets from another signal when that source changes, but the user can still overwrite it.

const options = signal(['a', 'b']);
const selected = linkedSignal(() => options()[0]);
selected.set('b'); // allowed; reset when options change

It replaces the old pattern of an effect that copies a source into a writable signal.

A pure pipe only runs when its input reference changes, so filtering with it will not update when an item is added to the same array. Making the pipe impure fixes that but then it runs on every change detection, for every row.

With a large list this is slow. Filter in the component with a computed signal instead, so it recomputes only when the list or filter changes.

With SSR, the server sends ready HTML. Hydration lets Angular reuse that DOM instead of destroying and rebuilding it on the client, which avoids the flicker and the extra work, and improves Largest Contentful Paint.

Enable it with provideClientHydration(). Code that touches the DOM directly can break it, so use Angular's rendering and afterNextRender.

When state is large and shared across many unrelated parts, many developers must follow strict patterns, you need time-travel debugging or an audit trail of actions, or complex side effects need clear structure.

For most apps, services with signals (or NgRx SignalStore, a lighter option) are enough. Do not add NgRx because it is popular; it brings actions, reducers and effects that cost real code.

Rarely. Standalone is the default and the recommended style. A reason to keep a module is a large existing code base you migrate later, a library that still ships modules, or forRoot style APIs of older third-party libraries.

Some teams also keep a module as a way to group a feature's providers, but functions such as provideX() and route-level providers do that now. For new code, do not write NgModules.

Create a plain constant array with the common standalone pieces and spread it into each imports list.

export const SHARED = [NgOptimizedImage, DatePipe, ButtonComponent] as const;
@Component({ standalone: true, imports: [SHARED], ... })

Keep such bundles small; large bundles bring back the hidden dependencies that standalone was designed to remove.

Provider functions: provideRouter(routes), provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([...])), provideAnimations(). They are placed in the providers array of bootstrapApplication or ApplicationConfig.

They are tree-shakable and typed, and library authors now write provideXyz() instead of XyzModule.forRoot().

code.title: switchMap and inner catchError

followUps:
An error in the outer stream ends it, and the whole stream stops. If catchError is on the inner request instead, only that one request fails and the outer stream (for example typing in a search box) keeps working.

input$.pipe(switchMap(q => http.get(q).pipe(catchError(() => of([])))))

Put catchError inside switchMap to keep the stream alive; put it outside when you want it to end.

An HTTP observable is cold: each subscriber starts its own request. Two subscribe calls, or two uses of the async pipe on the same observable, send two requests.

Fix: subscribe once and store the result in a signal, use toSignal, or share the stream with shareReplay({ bufferSize: 1, refCount: true }). Using a cache service is also common.

forkJoin waits for all observables to complete and emits once with the last values, like Promise.all. It is good for several one-time requests. combineLatest emits every time any source emits, after each has emitted at least once, and does not need to complete.

Use forkJoin for load-once data, combineLatest for live values such as filters and search text. A forkJoin with a never-completing source never emits.

code.title: Default vs OnPush change detection

followUps:
It is a development-mode error that means a value changed during change detection, after Angular had already rendered it. In dev, Angular checks twice and finds the second value different.

Common cause: a child changes something that the parent's template already used, or a getter returns a new value each time (like new Date()). Fix by updating state earlier (in a lifecycle hook before render), using signals, or restructuring so data flows one way.

A method in a template runs on every change detection pass, which can be many times per second, for every instance. If the method does a loop, sort or filter, the cost multiplies.

Example: {{ getTotal() }} over 1000 rows runs 1000 times per check. Use a computed signal, a pure pipe, or compute once when the data changes. Cheap getters are fine.

markForCheck() marks this component and its parents as needing a check at the next normal change detection run. detectChanges() runs change detection right now for this component and its children.

Use markForCheck after data changes outside Angular's knowledge in an OnPush component (it is what the async pipe does). Use detectChanges sparingly; calling it often can hurt performance. Signals make both mostly unnecessary.

code.title: Auth interceptor with single refresh

followUps:
Keep one shared refresh observable. The first 401 starts the refresh; the other requests wait for it and then retry with the new token.

refresh$ ??= auth.refresh().pipe(shareReplay(1), finalize(() => refresh$ = null));
return refresh$.pipe(switchMap(() => next(addToken(req))));

Otherwise ten refresh calls race, and a one-time refresh token may be rejected on the second use.

Because any other host would receive your access token. If you send it to a third party (a CDN, an analytics URL, an image host), that owner can read it and act as the user.

Check the request URL: add the header only when it starts with your own API base URL (or a list of allowed hosts). The same rule applies in React with an Axios or fetch wrapper.

The functional interceptor (HttpInterceptorFn) is just a function (req, next) => ... registered with provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([authInterceptor])). It uses inject() for services, and needs less code than a class.

The class-based one implements HttpInterceptor and is registered with the HTTP_INTERCEPTORS token; it is still supported through withInterceptorsFromDi(). New code should use functions.

code.title: Subscription leak and unsubscribe

followUps:
Right after the other operators, and as the last operator in the pipe. If something with its own subscription, like switchMap, comes after takeUntil, the inner stream can keep running after the signal.

source$.pipe(switchMap(...), takeUntil(this.destroy$)).subscribe();

A lint rule (rxjs/no-unsafe-takeuntil) checks this. takeUntilDestroyed() is the modern version.

It can. shareReplay(1) without refCount: true keeps the source subscription open for ever, even when nobody listens, so a long-lived source keeps running and holds memory.

Use shareReplay({ bufferSize: 1, refCount: true }) so the source unsubscribes when the last subscriber leaves. For a cache that should live for the whole app, keeping it open is on purpose.

Reproduce the leak, then compare memory with Chrome DevTools. Take a heap snapshot, navigate to the screen and away several times, force garbage collection, and take another snapshot. Count instances of the component class: it should return to zero.

The Memory tab's "allocation timeline" also shows what is retained. For regression, add a unit test that destroys the component and checks that the subject has no observers.

Start by enabling it in a test or a branch and see what stops updating. Zoneless means Angular is told about changes only by signals, the async pipe, markForCheck, event handlers and the like, not by patching all async APIs.

Components that mutate plain fields from a timer, a promise or a third-party callback will no longer update. Search for those patterns and for libraries that use NgZone.run; the OnPush plus signals style already works.

Tests no longer rely on zone-based automatic detection. You call await fixture.whenStable() or use signals and fixture.detectChanges() explicitly. Code that used fakeAsync and tick() needs changes, since fakeAsync depends on zone.js.

Provide provideZonelessChangeDetection() in the test setup, and write tests that wait for stability rather than for time.

Angular tracks the pending work with an internal task tracker (PendingTasks) rather than zone.js. The server waits until the application is stable, meaning no pending tasks such as HTTP calls, and then serializes the HTML.

If you start your own async work that must be awaited before rendering, wrap it with PendingTasks so SSR waits for it. Otherwise the page may be sent before the data arrives.

Move from opinions to a short, written decision with criteria and a time limit. List what matters (team skills, hiring, long-term support, ecosystem, accessibility, performance, fit with the .NET back end), score the options, and run a small proof of concept for the same real feature in each.

Write an ADR (architecture decision record) with the result and the reasons. As lead, listen to both sides, decide when the time is up, and make sure the losing side is heard and the choice can be revisited after a review date.

With tools, not meetings. Use ESLint rules such as @nx/enforce-module-boundaries, or dependency-cruiser or Sheriff, to forbid forbidden imports (for example a feature importing another feature's internals). Only allow imports through each library's public index.ts.

Run these rules in CI so a violation fails the pull request, and use CODEOWNERS for shared libraries. Rules that only live in a document get broken.

When several teams must release independently on different schedules, the product is large with clear business areas, and you accept the cost. A micro-frontend means separate builds, shared design system, version management for shared dependencies and harder end-to-end testing.

For one or two teams it is usually too much; a well-organised monorepo with module boundaries (for example Nx) gives most of the benefit with far less complexity. Decide based on team structure, not on fashion.
